# 0. Identification

The decision is **SAN-2026-009** of **21 July 2026** by the *formation restreinte* of the **CNIL** (French data protection authority). It is a **penalty decision** with a **public version** and the organisation name (**HOPITAL PRIVE DE LA LOIRE**) is visible. The status is "appeal possible; to be checked". In one sentence: the CNIL fines **HOPITAL PRIVE DE LA LOIRE** **€500,000** for breaches of **GDPR Articles 32 (security) and 34 (communication of a personal data breach)** following a **June–July 2025 cyberattack** that exposed **524,867 patient records** and **202,246 records of designated trusted third parties** [header](cite:1) [operative part, 1st indent](cite:2).

---

---

# 1. Facts

## Who
The sanctioned organisation is **HOPITAL PRIVE DE LA LOIRE**, a *société anonyme* (public limited company) created on **1 January 1970**, registered at the **Saint-Étienne** Trade and Companies Register under number **704 501 006**, and headquartered at **39, boulevard de la Palle, Saint-Étienne (42100)** [§ 1](cite:3). It is part of the **RAMSAY SANTE group**, described as the leader in private hospitalisation and primary care in Europe and the **leading private healthcare actor in France, Sweden, Denmark and Norway** [§ 2](cite:4).

Between **July 2023 and June 2024**, the hospital generated **€91.8 million** in revenue with a **net loss of €2.9 million**; between **July 2024 and June 2025**, it generated **€93.4 million** in revenue with a **net loss of €5.2 million** [§ 3](cite:5). The group’s revenue and profit figures for **July 2024–June 2025** are **redacted** [§ 3](cite:6).

The hospital employs **566 full-time equivalent staff**, including **about 15 doctors**, and has a medical community of **about 200 self-employed practitioners** (surgeons, doctors, physiotherapists, midwives) linked to the hospital by practice contracts [§ 4](cite:7).

The case originated from a **data breach notification** by the hospital to the CNIL on **4 July 2025** [§ 13](cite:8). The CNIL also received **nine complaints** from individuals affected by the breach [§ 14](cite:9).

The people affected are:
- **Patients**: **530,000** in the DPI in **2025** [§ 7](cite:10).
- **Designated trusted third parties**: **202,246** individuals whose data was also exfiltrated [§ 12](cite:11) [§ 137](cite:12).

The hospital **did not individually inform** the **202,246 trusted third parties** of the breach [§ 137](cite:13).

## What
The processing at issue is the **Dossier Patient Informatisé (DPI)**, a centralised electronic patient record system used to trace patient care pathways and coordinate healthcare interventions. It is managed via a **web application** accessible with a **username and password**, and patient files can be accessed via a **URL containing a patient-specific identifier** [§ 5](cite:14).

The **data concerned** in the DPI includes:
- **Administrative data**: patient file number, title, first and last names, date and place of birth, sex, **social security number**, postal address, **permanent patient identifier (IPP)**, marital status, professional status, identity and contact details of a designated trusted person, and in some cases, **a copy of the front of the national identity card** of the patient, their guardian, or legal representative for minors [§ 7](cite:15).
- **Biometric data**: security photograph [§ 7](cite:16).
- **Health data**: nursing, medical, and paramedical observations before and during hospitalisation, including **reasons for hospitalisation, consultation lists, and anaesthesia-related information** [§ 7](cite:17).

The **incident** occurred between **26 June and 1 July 2025**, when an attacker **gained access to the DPI** using the credentials of a **self-employed doctor** linked to the hospital. The attacker **exfiltrated 524,867 patient files**, including:
- **46,185 files** containing a **copy of the front of the national identity card** [§ 12](cite:18).
- **43 files** containing **health data** [§ 12](cite:19).
- **202,246 files** containing data on **designated trusted third parties** (relationship, name, first name, phone number) [§ 12](cite:20).

The **risks and harm** identified by the CNIL include:
- The breach is **"de nature à créer un préjudice moral et matériel"** [likely to cause non-material and material harm] for the individuals concerned, exposing them to **data resale, identity theft, and phishing** [§ 49](cite:21).
- The **unauthorised disclosure of health data** can have serious consequences, such as **damage to reputation, integrity, or discrimination** in employment, housing, or insurance [§ 49](cite:22).
- The CNIL admits that it is **"pas possible de déterminer avec certitude"** [not possible to determine with certainty] that the frauds reported by complainants stem from this breach [§ 50](cite:23).

The hospital had **no prior penalties or formal notices** cited in the decision.

## Where
The territory is **France**. The decision does not mention European cooperation or a one-stop-shop mechanism.

## When
- **Period of the breach**: **26 June to 1 July 2025** [§ 12](cite:24).
- **Discovery of the incident**: **1 July 2025**, following an alert from a self-employed doctor unable to connect to the DPI [§ 10](cite:25).
- **Notification to the CNIL (Art. 33)**: **4 July 2025** [§ 13](cite:26).
- **Information of individuals (Art. 34)**: The hospital informed its **patients** via a **press release on its website**, **126,000 personalised emails**, **210,000 SMS**, and **88,000 postal letters** between **July and August 2025** [§ 135](cite:27). The **202,246 trusted third parties** were **not informed** [§ 137](cite:28).
- **On-site inspection**: **29 July 2025** [§ 15](cite:29).
- **Report notified to the hospital**: **1 August 2025** [§ 15](cite:30).
- **Rapporteur appointed**: **19 February 2026** [§ 17](cite:31).
- **Sanction report served**: **5 March 2026** [§ 18](cite:32).
- **Hospital’s written observations**: **3 April 2026** [§ 19](cite:33).
- **Closure of investigation**: **18 May 2026** [§ 20](cite:34).
- **Hearing**: **18 June 2026** [§ 22](cite:35).
- **Decision date**: **21 July 2026** [header](cite:36).

---
---
# 2. Procedure

The procedure was **ordinary** (not simplified). The case began with the hospital’s **breach notification** on **4 July 2025** and the CNIL’s receipt of **nine complaints** [§ 14](cite:37). The CNIL conducted an **on-site inspection** on **29 July 2025** [§ 15](cite:38). The hospital provided **additional elements** on **4 August 2025** [§ 16](cite:39).

The president of the CNIL appointed a *rapporteure* on **19 February 2026** [§ 17](cite:40). The *rapporteure* served a **sanction report** on **5 March 2026**, proposing a fine, an injunction with a *astreinte* (periodic penalty), and **publication with anonymisation after two years** [§ 18](cite:41). The hospital submitted **written observations** on **3 April 2026** [§ 19](cite:42). The investigation closed on **18 May 2026**, and the hospital was informed of the hearing date [§ 20](cite:43). The *formation restreinte* heard **oral observations** on **18 June 2026** [§ 22](cite:44).

The decision does not mention any **procedural objections** raised by the company. It cites **CNIL precedents** (SAN-2021-020, SAN-2020-014, SAN-2019-005, SAN-2018-011) and **CJEU case law** (C-340/21, C-687/21, C-807/21, C-383/23) [§ 37, 38, 146, 147](cite:45).

---
---
# 3. Legal basis

The *formation restreinte* establishes the following breaches:
- **Article 32 GDPR (security of processing)**: multiple failures in technical and organisational measures, including:
  - **Absence of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or VPN for remote access** by external users (self-employed practitioners, their secretaries, and the software editor’s staff) [§ 61](cite:46).
  - **Inadequate access rights policy**: no **compartmentalisation of patient files** by care team, allowing access to **all patient records** regardless of involvement in care [§ 77](cite:47).
  - **Insufficient traceability measures**: no **automated real-time analysis of application logs** to detect abnormal activity [§ 94](cite:48).
  - **Non-compliance with password secrecy** during the **post-breach reset procedure**: a **single temporary password** was shared with all external users via an intermediary [§ 107](cite:49).
  - **Uncontrolled access by the software editor**: the editor had **permanent, unsupervised remote access** to the DPI and patient data [§ 116](cite:50).

- **Article 34 GDPR (communication of a personal data breach)**: failure to **directly inform the 202,246 designated trusted third parties** whose data was also exfiltrated [§ 131](cite:51).

No breaches were **rejected** by the *formation restreinte*.

---
---
# 4. Arguments

The company argues that its **password policy complied with CNIL and ANSSI recommendations** and that it had **planned and engaged** a trajectory to secure remote access via a multi-factor authentication platform (**[…]**) before the breach, with deployment completed in **September 2025** [§ 62](cite:52). It also highlights its **efforts to modernise its IT system**, including participation in the **HospiConnect** and **Care** programmes [§ 63](cite:53).

The company further argues that the **temporary password reset procedure** was justified by **urgency** to stop the ongoing breach without disrupting care continuity, as the software did not allow **individualised automated resets** [§ 108](cite:54). It claims this was the **only available technical solution** [§ 108](cite:55).

Regarding **access by the software editor**, the hospital argues that **permanent access** was necessary for **rapid and effective support** under a **third-party maintenance agreement**. It states that permanent access was only for **maintenance**, while advanced technical administration required connection via a **bastion server** where all activity is logged [§ 117](cite:56).

For the **Article 34 breach**, the hospital argues that the **data of trusted third parties was partial** (limited to name, first name, phone number, relationship) and **not structured**, reducing its exploitability. It claims its **risk assessment** concluded that the breach did not present a **high risk** to these individuals, so **no communication was required** [§ 134–135](cite:57).

The company also argues that the **proposed fine is disproportionate** given its **financial situation** and that of the **RAMSAY SANTE group**. It cites **mitigating circumstances**, including **cooperation with the CNIL**, **measures taken to mitigate harm**, the **non-deliberate nature** of the breaches (linked to technical and organisational constraints of legacy software), and the **absence of direct harm** reported to the CNIL [§ 150](cite:58).

The *formation restreinte* **rejects** these arguments:
- The **absence of MFA or VPN** for external users **did not meet the security requirements** of the **health sector’s electronic identification framework**, which mandates **two-factor authentication for remote access** [§ 65](cite:59).
- The **lack of compartmentalisation** of patient files **violated the care team principle** under **Articles L. 1110-4 and L. 1110-12 of the Public Health Code**, which restricts access to patient data to those **directly involved in care** [§ 82–85](cite:60).
- The **insufficient traceability** measures **failed to detect the attacker’s abnormal activity** over **five days**, during which **524,867 files were exfiltrated** [§ 97](cite:61).
- The **temporary password reset procedure** **violated password secrecy** by using a **single shared password** transmitted via an intermediary [§ 110](cite:62).
- The **permanent, uncontrolled access** by the software editor **exceeded the necessities of its mission** and **compromised data confidentiality** [§ 121](cite:63).
- The **failure to inform trusted third parties** was **unjustified**, as their data (name, first name, phone number, relationship) **posed a high risk** of **phishing and identity theft**, especially when combined with patient data [§ 139](cite:64).

**Remaining weak points**:
- The CNIL **admits uncertainty** about whether the **frauds reported by complainants** stem from this breach: it is **"pas possible de déterminer avec certitude"** [not possible to determine with certainty] [§ 50](cite:65).
- The hospital’s **AIPD (2021)** had identified the **lack of compartmentalisation** as a **major threat** but judged its **likelihood as limited** [§ 84](cite:66).

---
---
# 5. Decision

## Fine
The *formation restreinte* imposes a **fine of €500,000** for breaches of **Articles 32 and 34 GDPR** [operative part, 1st indent](cite:67). The fine is **not split by breach** in the operative part.

The **factors** used to set the fine (Art. 83 GDPR) include:
- **Gravity**: the breaches affected **524,867 patients and 202,246 trusted third parties**, involved **special-category data (health data)**, and **facilitated a large-scale breach** [§ 154](cite:68).
- **Negligence**: the hospital **failed to implement basic security measures** (MFA, VPN, compartmentalisation, log analysis) despite **knowing the risks** (AIPD 2021) [§ 161](cite:69).
- **Categories of data**: the DPI contained **health data (Art. 9 GDPR)** and **copies of identity documents**, requiring **enhanced protection** [§ 167](cite:70).
- **Financial capacity**: the fine is calculated based on the **RAMSAY SANTE group’s turnover** (as a single economic unit under EU competition law) to ensure it is **effective, proportionate, and dissuasive** [§ 172](cite:71).

## Injunction and *astreinte*
The *formation restreinte* orders the hospital to:
1. **Implement a system for proactive real-time or short-term analysis of application logs** to detect abnormal user behaviour and trigger alerts, within **3 months**, under a **periodic penalty (*astreinte*) of €1,000 per day of delay** [operative part, 2nd indent, 1st bullet](cite:72).
2. **Update its access rights policy** to comply with **Articles L. 1110-4 and L. 1110-12 of the Public Health Code** (care team principle), including a **break-glass mechanism** for emergencies, within **15 months**, under a **periodic penalty of €1,000 per day of delay** [operative part, 2nd indent, 2nd bullet](cite:73).
3. **Implement technical measures** to ensure the software editor’s access to the DPI is **only granted with prior hospital authorisation**, within **3 months**, under a **periodic penalty of €1,000 per day of delay** [operative part, 2nd indent, 3rd bullet](cite:74).

## Publication
The decision will be **published on the CNIL’s website and Légifrance** and will **no longer identify the hospital by name after two years** [operative part, 3rd indent](cite:75).

---
---
# 6. Appeal

The decision is **susceptible to appeal before the Conseil d’État**. The **deadline to appeal is to be checked by the tool** [end of decision](cite:76). The decision **does not state whether an appeal has been lodged**.
